item.title: Higher Order Unfitted Discontinuous Galerkin Methods in Space and Time
item.dc:creator: Fabian Heimann, Christoph Lehrenfeld
item.description:
Stability, well-posedness and a priori error derivations from an assumed list of discrete inequalities are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with an AI assistant.
We present and analyse an unfitted space-time discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method of arbitrary order for convection-diffusion problems on moving domains in up to three space dimensions. The method is discontinuous in space and time and uses upwind fluxes, so that convection is stabilised without additional terms and a Ghost penalty is needed only in the vicinity of the moving boundary. We prove inf-sup stability in a problem-specific norm, which in addition to the coercive part controls the time derivative in the diffusion-dominated regime and the material derivative in the convection-dominated regime. From this we derive a priori error estimates of high order in space and time for both regimes, including vanishing diffusion. Numerical experiments confirm the convergence rates and the robustness with respect to the diffusion coefficient.

item.title: Vx: A Programming Language for Scalable, Maintainable and Secure Systems
item.dc:creator: Aditya Kumar
item.description:
Lean 4 proofs (60 files, 777 theorems, no sorry) establish data-race freedom, DRF-SC, and scheduler properties for model languages of Vx's concurrency checks.
A program for a modern machine runs on several kinds of chips. Its memory spaces, links and capacities are invisible to the compilers of today. So a host that reads device memory, a working set that does not fit, or a data race shows up only when the program runs. Vx is a systems programming language that puts these facts in the program text. A machine is a source file of declarations. A value's type says which memory it lives in. Apart from one stated exception, a function's signature is the whole contract that its callers see. A flag lists the code and the facts that the compiler trusts without a proof. This report is a tour of the language at one commit. It describes six design principles, the core language, and the features that serve three qualities. Vx is scalable because one program text runs across machines, cores and GPU threads. With an option, the compiler also checks its function bodies in parallel. It is maintainable because a signature is the contract of a function and most diagnostics have codes. The output of the parallel compiler does not depend on the number of threads. It is secure because safe code has ownership, borrow, race and placement checks, and in safe code, a file or a socket of the standard library opens only with a right. For every feature, the report gives its status and the evidence for it. It also lists where the implementation does not yet meet the design.

item.title: Stokes corners and the global structure of steady rotating waves in annular domains
item.dc:creator: Quan Wang
item.description:
Polynomial identities, factorizations and inequalities in a key algebraic step are machine-checked in Lean 4 (file AnnularStokes.lean); the analytic results remain unformalized.
We study steady rotating water waves in a planar annulus, in the model of radial gravity and constant vorticity introduced by Li and the author. The stream function is harmonic, and the free surface carries the Bernoulli condition $p_0^2|\nablaΨ|^2=Q_α(S)$ with $Q_α(R)=(R-r_-)(R-r_+)$. We first settle the crest shape. For $α\neqα_\pm$, every stagnation point lies on the circle $R=r_-$, and the surface forms a symmetric $120^\circ$ corner there. At $α=α_\pm$ the corner is a right angle. The same holds for limits of smooth solutions and, in the lower region, for overhanging waves. We then study the global bifurcation continuum. Its waves are monotone from crest to trough, and they always cross the laminar circle. Hence there is no secondary bifurcation, and the parameter stays above an explicit floor. The continuum ends in an extreme wave, overturns, or degenerates; the last case is excluded for $c_0>γ^2e^{2γ}/(1+γ)^2$. An annular Nekrasov equation and an invariant Keady–Norbury cone give a slope bound below $90^\circ$ whenever the Nekrasov weight is nonnegative on the waves. A sharpened angular flow-force estimate keeps the troughs where this weight is nonnegative, for every $γ\in(0,1)$ above the floor. Hence, whenever $c_0>γ^2e^{2γ}/(1+γ)^2$, the existence half of the Stokes conjecture holds: the continuum contains an extreme wave with a $120^\circ$ Stokes crest. In the remaining band $\sinh^2γ<c_0\leγ^2e^{2γ}/(1+γ)^2$ the result is conditional: the continuum ends in such a wave unless its parameter degenerates to the value at which the effective gravity vanishes on the stagnation circle, and we cannot exclude this degeneration. We also show that the bifurcation is supercritical for every $γ\in(0,1)$.

item.title: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication
item.dc:creator: Vian Robotin, Jérémie Decouchant, Shaokang Xie, Dakai Kang, Mohammad Sadoghi
item.description:
Impossibility results and the safety and liveness of both Pearl protocol variants are machine-checked in Lean 4 on a model of the protocols.
Recent research has investigated fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus. An orthogonal line of work has demonstrated that equipping replicas with trusted execution environments (TEEs) enables more efficient consensus protocols with only $2f{+}1$ replicas. In this work, we bridge these two areas and demonstrate that two key fair-ordering properties, ordering linearizability and $γ$-batch-order fairness with minimal batching, cannot be implemented in partially synchronous networks with $2f{+}1$ replicas, even when the replicas are equipped with TEEs. We show that Byzantine replicas can circumvent TEE protections by manipulating the timing of transaction submissions to the enclave, thereby biasing the resulting ordering indicators. However, we prove that assuming a synchronous network allows both properties to be implemented with a reduced replica count. We propose two mechanisms: one uses absolute TEE-attested timestamps to guarantee ordering linearizability in a system of $n \ge 2f{+}1$ replicas, and the other uses TEE-maintained relative sequence numbers to guarantee $γ$-batch-order fairness when $n > \frac{2γf}{2γ-1}$. Ultimately, we integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm, achieving strong fair-ordering properties and superior performance while requiring fewer replicas than representative state-of-the-art baselines.

item.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
item.dc:creator: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Franz Franchetti, Karthik Duraisamy, Jeffrey Vetter, Yohann Dudouit
item.description:
Uses AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Aristotle) to formalize scientific-computing proofs in Lean with Mathlib and TorchLean, analyzing failure modes.
Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

item.title: Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals
item.dc:creator: Paco Navarro, Michael Emmerich
item.description:
The logical skeleton of the NP-hardness reduction for pinned Coulomb crystals is machine-checked in Lean 4 as a conditional correctness theorem.
Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.

item.title: The Geometry of Banach space operator-valued measures with cyclic dilations
item.dc:creator: Daniel Freeman, Qianfeng Hu, Rui Liu, Jie Shen
item.description:
Main results on operator-valued measures and cyclic dilations were formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4, with 70 literature results assumed as axioms; repository provided.
In this paper, we investigate the geometric properties of operator-valued measures with cyclic dilations. Under a localization condition on the normal part of the bidual, we establish James-type characterizations of shrinking, bounded completeness, and reflexivity for projection-valued measures. These characterizations apply to spaces admitting no continuous Schauder frame, including $L_1[0,1]$. Using vector measure representations and interpolation, we prove that an operator-valued measure admitting a cyclic dilation has a reflexive cyclic dilation if and only if the underlying space is reflexive. Under the same cyclicity assumption, we also characterize the existence of cyclic dilations on spaces containing no $\ell_1$ and on KB-spaces. The dilation spaces can be chosen to be order-continuous Köthe function spaces. Without assuming cyclicity, we give a weak compactness criterion and local variation conditions for reflexive dilations; an example on $\ell_2$ shows that reflexivity alone is insufficient. For a separable space containing no $c_0$, a normalized operator-valued measure is induced by a continuous Schauder frame if and only if it admits a cyclic dilation and has $σ$-finite operator-norm variation. Finally, for measure quotients whose synthesis maps admit bounded linear right inverses, we construct compatible cyclic $L_p$-dilations and represent the quotient spaces as inductive limits, with applications to ReLU Barron spaces.

item.title: Area Stability for Largest Small Polygons
item.dc:creator: José Ayala Hoffmann, Joaquín López Gutiérrez
item.description:
Selected linear algebra results supporting the interval-arithmetic spectral verification (Neumann bound, inertia identities, Gershgorin criterion) are formalised in Lean 4 within the LSPectra artifact.
We develop a second order calculus for area maximisation among small polygons of diameter at most one, culminating in rigorous computational proofs of stationarity, spectral stability and strict local maximality modulo orientation preserving Euclidean motions for the polygons $Q_n$, whose diameter graphs consist of a cycle on $n-1$ vertices and one pendant edge, for every even $n$ with $6\le n\le 64$. At a stationary configuration, positive multipliers force first order area decrease along feasible directions that shorten at least one active diameter. Along directions that preserve all active diameters to first order, the reduced Hessian governs second order area change modulo Euclidean motions. Positive multipliers, independent active constraint gradients, and a negative reduced spectrum imply strict local maximality. Outward rounded interval arithmetic establishes existence of strictly convex stationary configurations $Q_n$ with all $n-3$ reduced eigenvalues strictly negative. Together, these results yield explicit neighbourhood radii and rigorous quadratic area decrease bounds for all sufficiently nearby feasible polygons. The reduced spectrum also detects second order degeneracy and instability, as illustrated by an optimal quadrilateral and the regular hexagon.

item.title: VeriLogic: Reinforcement Learning over Verifiable Logical Reasoning Traces
item.dc:creator: ZeLiang Chen, Yunyao Zhang, Xinglang Zhang, Wenbing Li, Junqing Yu, Zikai Song
item.description:
Translates natural-language logic problems into Lean4 premises and goals, using Lean4 proof checking as an RL reward signal and for iterative proof repair.
Logical reasoning derives conclusions from premises through explicit intermediate inference steps, providing a natural basis for process-level verification and supervision. However, existing learning methods often rely on response-level outcome signals, which overlook heterogeneous correctness within the reasoning trace: a correct answer may contain invalid reasoning, while valid intermediate steps may also appear in an incorrect response. To address this issue, we introduce Reinforcement Learning on Verifiable Logical Reasoning (VeriLogic), which turns internal reasoning traces into explicit and verifiable learning objects. Rather than treating a response as an indivisible learning unit, VeriLogic decomposes logical reasoning into explicit intermediate judgments, proofs, and final decisions, and organizes them into a unified "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline: (1) Verification-Grounded Reasoning Environment Construction grounds logical reasoning into explicit intermediate states and formally checkable proof obligations, making the internal reasoning process accessible to verification and learning; (2) Logical Structured Policy Optimization learns from verifier feedback through complementary global and local rewards, jointly optimizing the overall reasoning outcome while providing targeted optimization signals to different intermediate reasoning paths; and (3) Verifier-Guided Iterative Refinement acts on verifier feedback by leveraging proof states and error messages to iteratively diagnose and repair failed reasoning. Experiments on six logical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, with average improvements of 6.39% and 5.00% on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1. These results highlight the value of making logical reasoning traces verifiable, learnable, and refinable beyond final-answer supervision.

item.title: On the tensor product of semistable Hermitian adelic vector bundles over an adelic curve
item.dc:creator: Huayi Chen, Yijun Yuan
item.description:
The paper's results, including tensor semistability and the Bost conjecture specialization, are formalized sorry-free in Lean 4 using Mathlib.
We prove tensor semistability for Hermitian adelic vector bundles on proper adelic curves whose underlying fields are countable and of characteristic zero. The central estimate concerns the canonical integral Specht lattice of a rectangular partition with fixed height: its logarithmic covolume, divided by its rank and tensor degree, tends to zero. We prove this estimate from monic seminormal norms and an exact hypergeometric law weighted by the square of a Vandermonde product for tableau prefixes. Constant adelic Specht bundles and equivariant contractions then yield the slope inequality for every geometrically semistable subspace of a finite tensor product. The correction is the measure of the Archimedean places times a sublinear Specht term and vanishes in the limit as the auxiliary degree tends to infinity. An instability-filtration argument completes the reduction to arbitrary factors and identifies the tensor product Harder–Narasimhan filtration. The number field specialization gives the Bost tensor semistability conjecture in all ranks.

item.title: Schur decomposition with logarithmic precision in cubic time up to logarithmic factors
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Colbrook
item.description:
The main theorem on the randomised Schur decomposition algorithm (logarithmic precision, cubic time) has been formally verified in Lean, cited as a separate artifact.
How much arithmetic precision is needed to compute a Schur decomposition to a prescribed tolerance? Let $A$ be a complex matrix of order $n$ with spectral norm at most one, let $0<δ<1/2$ be the tolerance, and let $0<p<1/2$ be the requested failure probability. Our randomised floating-point algorithm uses $O(\log(n/(δp)))$ mantissa bits per real component and $O(n^3\log^2(n/(δp)))$ arithmetic operations on every execution, with universal constants. It returns $Q$ and an exactly upper triangular $T$. With probability at least $1-p$, both $\|A-QTQ^*\|_2$ and $\|Q^*Q-I\|_2$ are at most $δ$. We sample a small perturbation using finitely many bits and use Gaussian estimates to bound the eigenvector conditioning and eigenvalue gap. A single contour estimate bounds the effect of a rounding error through any number of remaining Newton steps. At each subdivision level, the full matrix is unitarily similar to a small perturbation of the regularised input. This allows us to bound the conditioning of each diagonal block directly from that input and to use the same precision throughout.

item.title: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization
item.dc:creator: Tianjian Zhang, Cosme Louart, Malik Tiomoko, Zhenyu Liao
item.description:
A companion Lean 4/Mathlib package machine-checks the quantitative Gaussian comparison (Proposition C.4) and its concentration tools, with statement correspondence and sorry/axiom checks.
We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincaré inequality. Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.

item.title: On Robust Strictly Positive Real Synthesis for High-Order Interval Polynomials
item.dc:creator: Tiancheng Xu, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, ZhengTai Xiong, Long Wang, Wensheng Yu
item.description:
Both main theorems, the order-ten-and-higher counterexamples and the all-order synthesis result, are formally verified in Lean 4, with a public repository.
We establish two complementary results on common strictly positive real (SPR) numerators for Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial families. First, for every order $n \ge 10$, we construct a monic Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial family with rational endpoints and positive width in every nonleading coefficient such that every nonzero real numerator of degree at most $n$ produces a strictly negative real part at some member and some positive frequency. In particular, robust Hurwitz stability alone does not guarantee equal-degree SPR synthesis in high orders. Second, for every order $n \ge 1$, we prove that a common real SPR numerator of exact degree $n$ always exists whenever the lower endpoint of each interior coefficient interval is at most $10^{-5}$ times its upper endpoint, while the constant and leading coefficients vary over arbitrary compact positive intervals.

item.title: Territorial Conflict as a Cellular Automaton: Frozen Domains and Active Fronts in a Risk-Derived Local Rule
item.dc:creator: Maria Teresa Arias
item.description:
Formal properties of a Risk-derived cellular automaton (radius bounds, irreversibility, finite-time freezing, locality) are machine-checked in Lean 4 without sorry.
We formulate the attack and fortification rules of the game Risk as a synchronous cellular automaton on a graph, with battles resolved by exact dice odds. We prove, and verify in Lean, that for the default exchange ratio the rule has radius 6, or 5 for deterministic battles with a positive attack threshold, both attained; that its deterministic form is irreversible except at the highest attack thresholds without growth and with fortification absent or inactive; that without troop growth it freezes in finite time; and that the dynamics near an interface is locally determined. The coupling of the ownership field to a troop field separates frozen domains from active fronts: with a positive attack threshold, saturated domains cannot be conquered, while interfaces with heterogeneous troops keep fighting. In 14252 runs, with attractors classified operationally in Wolfram's scheme, raising the attack threshold takes the system from dominance by one faction to a frozen fragmented partition. The share of the largest faction drops between the same two threshold values at every size up to L=128, in a step about 0.5 wide under a continuous threshold (L=64-96), whereas the probability of complete consolidation is a size-dependent crossover governed by saturated minority domains. Long-period attractors combine spatially fixed local oscillators; apparent class-IV gliders are artefacts of index-ordered tie-breaking. Straight fronts stayed within two cells of their initial position for up to 500,000 steps, over which they are one-dimensional automata with non-recurrent, incompressible dynamics and positive Lyapunov speeds, constant for L>=48. Compared with mean-field and random-regular-graph controls, the lattice lengthens conflicts about twentyfold and clusters conquest: a cell next to a fresh conquest is about five times as likely as average to be conquered next, against 1.1-1.5 in the controls.

item.title: A Counterexample to Single-Control Null Controllability of Stochastic Heat Equations
item.dc:creator: Feizheng Huang, Zhaobo Liu
item.description:
The counterexample to single-control null controllability of stochastic heat equations comes with a Lean 4 formalization, published in a linked GitHub repository.
We disprove the conjecture that a single localized drift control suffices for null controllability of stochastic parabolic equations with bounded adapted coefficients. On a bounded interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, we construct a deterministic, nonnegative smooth noise coefficient supported at positive distance from the control interval. One fixed nonzero smooth initial state cannot be driven to zero almost surely at any positive time by any progressively measurable control with finite expected $L^2$ energy. The proof uses products of Brownian increments in the adjoint terminal data to keep the initial pairing bounded away from zero while the observation norm tends to zero. On the flat torus, the construction yields counterexamples in every Gevrey class of order $s>1$ whenever the complement of the control set contains an open ball. Thus Gevrey regularity above order one cannot replace analyticity as a general sufficient condition for null controllability.

item.title: The Equational Theory of Rational String-to-String Functions
item.dc:creator: Mikołaj Bojańczyk, Kacper Lewandowski, Katzper Michno
item.description:
The axiomatisation results were formalised in Lean, produced with the Aristotle (Harmonic) system, and the formalisation is publicly archived.
We give a sound and complete equational axiomatisation of the rational string-to-string functions, which can be seen as a transducer counterpart of the classical axiomatisations of regular languages by Salomaa [JACM'66], Krob [TCS'91], Bloom and Ésik [MSCS'93], and Kozen [IC'94]. The axioms are stated over a compositional, algebraic syntax for rational functions, namely the rational fragment of the syntax for regular functions introduced by Bojańczyk, Daviaud and Krishna [LICS'18]. The axiomatisation is finitary, as it consists of finitely many uniform families of axioms, each parameterised by the types involved. It is also purely equational: it consists only of equations, with no implication rules.

item.title: Degree-respecting labellings with ordered neighbour sums
item.dc:creator: Toshio Ishikawa, Tomoki Uda
item.description:
The proofs of the main theorem and corollary on degree-respecting graph labellings are checked in Lean 4.
In an exhaustive enumeration of hydrocarbons with only single bonds, carbon skeletons are generated as adjacency matrices and pruned by two rules: a vertex of larger degree receives a smaller label, and among vertices of equal degree, a vertex whose adjacency row is the larger binary integer receives a smaller label. The pruning is sound only if every skeleton admits a labelling obeying both rules. We prove that such a labelling exists for every finite simple graph, connected or not and with no bound on the degrees, and that the same holds when the weights $2^i$ of the labels $i$ are replaced by any strictly increasing real weights. The proof takes, among the labellings that order vertices by non-increasing degree, one minimising the sum over edges of the products of the endpoint weights.

item.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
item.dc:creator: Liang Song
item.description:
Twenty-eight Lean 4 + Mathlib modules (696 declarations, no sorry) mechanize sampling correctness, round-by-round soundness bounds, field-choice constraints, and executable verifiers.
Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.

item.title: Singularities in global pluripotential theory
item.dc:creator: Mingchen Xia
item.description:
All statements of the book on plurisubharmonic singularities are formalized in Lean 4, with acknowledged formalization help from collaborators.
This book is an expanded version of the author's lecture notes at the Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics (IASM) at Zhejiang University. We systematically develop the theory of plurisubharmonic singularities on compact Kähler manifolds and relate it to the non-Archimedean pluripotential theory and toric pluripotential theory.

item.title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model
item.dc:creator: Christopher Janjigian, Firas Rassoul-Agha, Timo Seppäläinen
item.description:
The paper's differentiability theorem for the last-passage percolation shape function is formalized in Lean 4 using AI-assisted autoformalization skills.
We prove that the shape function of planar directed last-passage percolation with general i.i.d.\ real-valued weights is differentiable on the open first quadrant, under a moment assumption of order $p''>4$ on the positive part of the weight and a nearly optimal order $p'>1$ on the negative part. Due to known results, only directions outside a percolation cone need be considered. The proof is a multiscale path-counting argument that uses the shape theorem, oriented percolation on a coarse-grained lattice, a simple change of measure in a finite region, and the van den Berg–Kesten inequality. Our Lean-formalized proof is an AI-assisted adaptation and improvement of the OpenAI proof of differentiability in planar first-passage percolation.

item.title: The smallest vertex triangle in a fixed polygon
item.dc:creator: Dawid Trela
item.description:
A Lean 4 project formalizes the unit-square upper bound 32/n^3 and its attainment at n=4k, plus finite estimates and the numerical witnesses.
Among the triangles determined by $n$ points in convex position in the unit square, one has area at most $32/n^3$. Equality is possible exactly when $4$ divides $n$, and then the maximizing point set is unique. We prove a fixed-container theorem for a class of convex $s$-gons that includes affinely regular polygons and a one-parameter family of pairwise affinely inequivalent hexagons without a centre of symmetry. If the container has equal ears of area $a$ and the tips of its directed side vectors are in convex position, the sharp bound at $n=sk$ is $a/k^3$. Its equality conditions determine every side vector of the maximizing polygon. The proof uses the area enclosed by the normalized side directions. We compare the result with the area-normalized smallest-ear theorem of Gronchi and Longinetti and give consequences for unrestricted Heilbronn configurations with 13 and 15 points.

item.title: Improving Razmyslov's (1974) bound: the Nagata-Higman index is at most $n^2-2$ for $n\ge3$
item.dc:creator: Dave Goel
item.description:
The Nagata-Higman bounds d(n) ≤ n²−1 and d(n) ≤ n²−2 were also proved in the Lean proof assistant.
Let $d(n)$ be the least $m$ such that every associative (not necessarily unital) algebra over a field of characteristic zero satisfying the identity $x^n=0$ also satisfies $x_1x_2\cdots x_m=0$; this is the Nagata-Higman index. Razmyslov proved $d(n)\le n^2$ in 1974; Kuzmin proved $d(n)\ge n(n+1)/2$ and conjectured equality; this is the Kuzmin (1975) conjecture. We prove $d(n)\le n^2-2$ for $n\ge3$ (and, by a simpler case of the same method, $d(n)\le n^2-1$ for $n\ge2$); in particular $d(6)\le34$. To our knowledge, $n=6$ is the first case in which the new bound improves the known bounds, and this is the first improvement of Razmyslov's bound for general $n$. For $m=n^2-1$ and $m=n^2-2$, Formanek's criterion reduces $d(n)\le m$ to the statement that no nonzero linear combination of $(m+1)$-cycles lies in one particular isotypic block of the group algebra of $S_{m+1}$. For $m=n^2-1$ this statement follows from the branching rule; for $m=n^2-2$ we prove it using the Jucys-Murphy elements and a theorem of Frobenius on the characters of the alternating group. These bounds have also been proved in the Lean proof assistant.

item.title: Subspaces of $L^1$ spanned by the even and odd levels of the Haar system
item.dc:creator: Thomas Speckhofer
item.description:
The proofs of the main theorem (the even-level Haar span is not isomorphic to L^1) and Corollary 3.4 were formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
We prove that the closed subspace of $L^1[0,1]$ spanned by the even (respectively, odd) levels of the Haar system is not isomorphic to $L^1[0,1]$. Moreover, the closed span of any infinite collection of Haar levels with infinite complement is isomorphic to that of the even levels.

item.title: Repeated Binary Direct Collinear Impacts Under Incremental Contact Laws With Residual Indentation: A Hybrid Systems Formulation
item.dc:creator: Mihails Milehins, Dan B. Marghitu
item.description:
Definitions and analytical properties of a hybrid-system impact model are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, largely written by Claude Code.
Incremental contact laws specify the normal contact force through a differential relation, possibly carrying an internal state, driven by the indentation and its rate. The force may vanish at a nonzero indentation, through plasticity, an elastic aftereffect, or, under some laws with a viscous component, a load drawing the bodies apart rapidly. Such a residual indentation sits uneasily within rigid body dynamics, which admits no deformation. The tension is tolerable when the indentation is small relative to the bodies, so that it may be carried constitutively rather than geometrically. Even then, the law alone does not determine the interaction: because force and indentation no longer vanish together, conditions for the commencement and termination of contact must be supplied separately, as must the fate of the deformation and internal state at separation, both absent from the equations of motion. This article formulates the repeated direct collinear impact of two convex axisymmetric bodies under continuous, bounded external forces as a hybrid system. The contact interface is modeled as a massless element carrying the contact law and its state, coupled to the bodies through relative velocity and an interaction force dictated by the contact state. Consequently, all switching and resets are confined to the interface, leaving the geometry and equations of motion of the bodies unaltered. The principal analytical properties of the formulation are established and formally verified in Lean 4 with the help of Claude by Anthropic. The framework is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

item.title: A Syntactic Approach to Ulmer's Bialgebras
item.dc:creator: David Forsman
item.description:
The paper's results on Ulmer's bialgebras in 2-categories with PIE limits are formalized in Lean 4, with a public artifact.
Ulmer proposed to view a bialgebraic structure on an object $x$ as a structure map $f\colon Fx\to Gx$ satisfying an equation $α_{(x,f)} = β_{(x,f)}$ of natural transformations. This perspective is powerful enough to account for many algebraic and coalgebraic structures, such as varieties of universal algebra, categories of algebras over a PROP, an operad or a monad. We develop Ulmer's bialgebras within a $2$-categorical setting with PIE limits, where structure maps are abstracted by inserters and their equations by equifiers. A syntax of signatures, theories and models is then used to produce these bialgebraic structures. The syntax of the commutative diagrams defining Hopf algebras can be used, as is, to define the $0$-cell of Hopf algebras within any symmetric pseudomonoid in a $2$-category with PIE limits. In this setting, we show that lax morphisms of models induce morphisms between the objects of algebras, extending the classical result lifting a lax monoidal functor to a functor between the categories of internal monoids. Since the construction of the object of bialgebras is expressed entirely in terms of PIE limits, we show that Kan extensions, accessibility, local presentability, orthogonal factorization systems, regularity, and Barr-exactness lift along the construction under suitable assumptions. A bi-dense class of objects allows us to transfer monadicity and local presentability results to formal settings. Finally, we construct a bi-dense class of $\V$-categories with at most three objects, where $\V$ is any monoidal category with an absorbing initial object.

item.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
item.dc:creator: Stefano Grassi
item.description:
Theorems 1–4 on incentive compatibility, potential-game equilibrium, and gradient convergence are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; source files are released.
Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$ and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.

item.title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
item.dc:creator: Gendo Kumoi, Hideki Yagi, Manabu Kobayashi, Shigeichi Hirasawa
item.description:
All lemmas, propositions and theorems on ECOC excess-error bounds and the reliability function are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided as ancillary files.
Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $κ\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $κ$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.

item.title: When Is Product Decoding of ECOC MAP-Consistent? Pair Structure and the n-vs-Rest Codes
item.dc:creator: Gendo Kumoi
item.description:
All theorems, lemmas, propositions and corollaries on ECOC decoder MAP-consistency are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided as arXiv ancillary files.
Error-Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) combine binary classifiers by the sum decoder, which totals probabilities, or the product decoder, which totals log-likelihoods. In the noiseless setting, where the binary classifiers output the true posteriors, we ask on which code matrices each decoder always agrees with the Bayes-optimal (MAP) class. For the sum decoder the answer is known: the code must be equidistant (James and Hastie, 1998). We answer the question for the product decoder. Two classes are compared through the votes of the columns on which they differ: the sum decoder decides by their sample mean, the product decoder by an M-estimator with influence function artanh, and each vote is the MAP margin plus a bias determined by the other classes alone. Our main theorem states that the product decoder is MAP-consistent if and only if, for every class pair, the columns on which the two classes differ are matched with the columns obtained by swapping the two classes (or their complements), and equivalently if and only if the code is a union of n-vs-Rest codes. Efficient equidistant codes are therefore excluded: Hadamard codes ($M\ge 8$), which meet the Plotkin bound with $M-1$ columns, have no such pairs, and for the Sylvester type the reversal margin can be at least a constant 0.0182 independent of $M$. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. On six real datasets with estimated probabilities, the product decoder is slightly more accurate when each column is calibrated, and the sum decoder is better when the calibration error differs across columns; in either case the decoders disagree only near ties.

item.title: Polynomial-Time Learning of Random Automata from One Label per Word
item.dc:creator: Yilin Cheng
item.description:
A Lean repository of 22 modules formalizes selected proof steps, including the four-source coefficient, deletion bounds, and finite counting inequalities.
We study a binary deterministic finite automaton whose $2n$ transitions are chosen independently and uniformly from its $n$ states. The learner observes independent uniform words of length $m$, each labeled with a single bit indicating acceptance. For every fixed $β>0$ we give a polynomial-time algorithm that works outside a set of transition tables of probability $o(n^{-β})$. On each remaining table, for any start state and accepting set, the predictor has error at most $ε$ on fresh uniform words of length $m$ with probability at least $1-γ$ over the training sample and the learner's random choices. Its sample size and running time are polynomial in $n$, $m$, $1/ε$ and $\log(2/γ)$, with degree depending only on $β$. Although each word reveals only one output, comparing label moments at two consecutive history lengths lets us estimate the expected product of the signed outputs of two continuations from the same hidden state. We also refute Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times. For two distinct states fixed before the table is drawn and every fixed $c>0$, the fraction of words of length $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ that send them to different states converges in probability to $e^{-c}$. On a typical table, driving this fraction down to $1/n$ takes asymptotically $n\log n$ letters. Selected proof steps are formalized in Lean.

item.title: The Wilson-loop formulation of Yang-Mills at finite mode truncation: a Level-Two structural bypass of the Gribov ambiguity
item.dc:creator: Yu. N. Berdinsky
item.description:
Nine theorems on the Wilson-loop formulation of truncated Yang-Mills are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with no sorry, admit or new axioms.
The unfixed real-time Henstock-Kurzweil functional integral for truncated Yang-Mills removes the choice of a gauge surface, but gauge orbits remain objects of the formulation: that is a Level-One bypass of the Gribov ambiguity. This paper carries out a Level-Two bypass at finite mode truncation: the Wilson loops W(C) are taken as the fundamental variables, so that the configuration space is a space of loop data and no gauge field, gauge orbit, gauge-fixing condition or Faddeev-Popov determinant occurs anywhere in the formulation. Nine statements are proved and machine checked in Lean 4 without sorry, without admit and without new axioms: the loop algebra is commutative, conjugation-closed and gauge invariant, with bounded generators and the SU(2) Mandelstam identity; the truncated Yang-Mills action is an affine polynomial in the plaquette Wilson variables; loop-expressible observables are cylindrical; the oscillatory integrand is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable on every bounded loop-space box for every calibration, with the Lebesgue value; the integral is independent of gauge-fixing data and gauge copies are the same point of the loop formulation; for loop observables the Level-Two integral with respect to the push-forward measure coincides with the Level-One unfixed integral; the one-plaquette SU(2) check is proved in full, including the closed form 2J_1(beta)/beta; the SU(N) Mandelstam relations are derived in covariant trace form; and the finite-M integrals are projectively compatible, their limit existing as a linear functional, not a measure. No continuum limit, mass gap, confinement or Makeenko-Migdal equation is claimed; the Giles reconstruction theorem is cited only. The honest report records exactly where each proof stops.

item.title: AI-assisted formal proofs for static and time-dependent density functional theory on lattices
item.dc:creator: Miguel A. L. Marques, Irene D'Amico, Stefano Pittalis
item.description:
All theorems on lattice DFT and TDDFT are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib (about 17,000 lines), with the code written with AI assistance.
The Hohenberg-Kohn theorem fails on lattices, where two potentials that differ by more than a constant can share a ground state. We prove that such potentials are exceptional. We consider spinless fermions on any connected lattice, at any filling other than empty or full, with hopping amplitudes of a common sign and any density-density interaction. The potentials whose ground state is shared with a potential differing by more than a constant lie in a closed, nowhere dense set of zero Lebesgue measure. The densities of non-degenerate shared ground states form a set of codimension at least two. The statement about the potentials also holds for the Kohn-Sham potential and for spin-density functional theory, where a uniform shift of the magnetic field is the only additional freedom. In time-dependent density functional theory on lattices, we show that not every ground state of a connected lattice can serve as the initial state of the density-potential map. A counterexample is the ground state of two fermions on a square that Penz and van Leeuwen found as a counterexample to the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem. For almost every static potential, however, every real ground state can serve as an initial state, also for spin-resolved densities. We also give formal proofs that the time-dependent Kohn-Sham potential exists, locally in time, for almost every static Kohn-Sham potential, and of known results: local existence and uniqueness of the time-dependent potential for an admissible initial state, continuation in time up to the boundary of the set of admissible states, and the convergence properties of a regularized Kohn-Sham iteration. All theorems and propositions are formalized in the proof assistant Lean 4 and checked by computer.

item.title: Hadwigerś Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions
item.dc:creator: Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled, Goran Žužić
item.description:
Formalizes the full proof of Hadwiger's covering conjecture in R^3 in Lean 4 with Mathlib (13,663 lines), checked against an 18-line challenge specification.
Let $K \subset \R^3$ be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of $\R^3$ with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that $K$ can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar $λ\in (0, 1)$ and translation vectors $v_1, \dots, v_8 \in \R^3$ such that \[ K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{8} (λK + v_i). \] This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of $\frac{2}{3} K$. For any convex body $K$ that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body $S = \frac{1}{2}(K - K)$ in John's position ($B^3 \subseteq S$) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies $8 \int_{S^2} h_S \, d\sigmatilde < 12$, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of $K$, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector $w_* \in S^2$ whose shadow boundary $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ on $K$ itself is a continuous closed curve of $S$-length strictly less than $12$. Splitting $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ into six contiguous arcs of $S$-length strictly less than $2$ and applying Helly's theorem in $\R^3$ illuminates each arc with one direction, while $\pm w_*$ illuminate the remainder of $\partial K$. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini 4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
item.dc:creator: Nawaf Bou-Rabee
item.description:
Main theorems (mixing bound and Hessian-necessity lower bound) and a Gaussian lower bound are formalized and checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; sources released on GitHub.
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a fixed integration time can fail to mix because of resonances, and randomizing the integration time removes them. We prove that Metropolis-adjusted HMC with velocity Verlet and random integration times mixes from a warm start in a number of transitions that does not depend on the condition number, for every integration-time law satisfying a Fourier condition that we call non-resonant; uniform, exponential and triangular laws are examples. For a target density proportional to $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and $L_H$-Lipschitz Hessian and $κ=L/m$, the number of gradient evaluations needed to reach a fixed total variation accuracy is, up to constants and logarithmic factors, $\sqrt{κd}+\sqrt{L_H}\,(d/m)^{3/4}$. This is the first square-root condition-number bound for this sampler beyond Gaussian targets. The proof converts relative-entropy contraction of the unadjusted proposal into a conductance bound for the adjusted chain, and shows that the integration-time law enters only through its characteristic function. Hessian regularity cannot be dropped for a fixed step size: without it there are targets in the class for which the cost is at least of order $κ^{2/3}$, up to logarithmic factors, even from a warm start.

item.title: Validity and maximum violation of the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound for linear stabilizer codes
item.dc:creator: Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim
item.description:
All proofs except cited MDS-length facts are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using Comparator challenge files; SAT refutations are also checked by the Lean kernel.
Entanglement-assisted quantum codes protect quantum information with entangled pairs shared in advance, and the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound of Brun, Devetak and Hsieh is the standard estimate of how many pairs they consume. Codes that violate it at large distance are known. For linear entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes, which include all qubit stabilizer codes of this kind, we determine when the bound holds and how far it can fail. The answer depends on how many qudits, together with the receiver's halves of the pairs, recover the logical qudits. If this number is less than twice the number of logical qudits, the bound holds, also for degenerate codes. If it is exactly twice that, the bound overstates the number of pairs by at most the length of the longest classical maximum distance separable (MDS) code of that dimension, minus the dimension. Codes carrying values and derivatives of polynomials on the projective line attain this maximum whenever the field size is at least that dimension and the MDS conjecture is known for it, which includes every prime and, by a recently announced result, every even field size. If the number is more than twice the number of logical qudits, the violation is bounded in terms of the lengths of classical codes of a given Singleton defect, and the bound is attained for one logical qudit. Apart from cited MDS lengths, the proofs are formalized in the Lean proof assistant.

item.title: The Anatomy of Piecewise-Linear Learned Indexes
item.dc:creator: Yue Chen, Yong Zhang
item.description:
Core probabilistic theorems on PLA learned-index fanout and hierarchy height are formalized in Lean 4/Mathlib in a 2,682-module library, PLAStochastic, with no sorrys.
Piecewise-linear approximation (PLA) learned indexes (PGM-index, FITing-Tree, RadixSpline, PLEX, PLIN) compress sorted keys into $\pm\varepsilon$ segments, yet prior theory stops at coarse $Θ(\varepsilon^2)$ single-segment bounds. At the bottom layer, optimal greedy PLA covers $κ_{\rm opt}\varepsilon^2/v_0 \approx 3.54\,\varepsilon^2/v_0$ keys per segment on independent gaps and $κ_{\rm opt}\varepsilon^2$ under any smooth density ($v_0=1$), while anchored and chord fitters retain $Θ(\varepsilon^2/v_0)$ coverage. Across recursive layers, a law-of-large-numbers heuristic–invoked to claim $O(\log\log n)$ height for the PGM-index–suggests summing $Θ(\varepsilon^2)$ gaps averages out fluctuations. We prove this fails under Endpoint Promotion (EP): stopping-time fluctuations reset relative gap variance at every depth, locking fanout at $C_\varepsilon \approx 19.861\,\varepsilon^2$, expected height at $\log n/\log C_\varepsilon + O(1)$, and lookup at $Θ(\log n)$. To break this barrier, Rank-Equispaced Promotion (RE) samples pivots at equal rank strides. Each stride sums a fixed number of base gaps, so relative variance decays across layers and cumulative coverage squares at each step. Expected height drops to $\log_2\log_\varepsilon n + O(1)$ on independent gaps and $\log_2\log_\varepsilon n + \log_2^+(\log n/\log(\varepsilon/δ)) + O(1)$ on smooth densities with curvature $δ$. A compact bucket directory routes across unaligned RE pivots with $<1$ extra comparison per layer on average, giving RE-PGM $O(\log\varepsilon \cdot \log\log_\varepsilon n)$ expected lookup in $Θ(n/\varepsilon^2)$ space and $O(n)$ build time without radix skew sensitivity. Our constants match empirical fanout within $0.3\%$ down to $\varepsilon=2$, and all core theorems are formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Nikolaou
item.description:
Writes 19 Lean 4/Mathlib proofs of three theorems and automatically extracts 18 dissimilarity measures from their elaborated terms and dependencies.
We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

item.title: Defining the mathematical family tree with a minimal programming language
item.dc:creator: Max Tegmark
item.description:
Definitions, key theorems, and model relations of a family tree of mathematical theories, plus the correctness of the MLISP language, are verified in Lean.
I introduce MLISP, a Turing-complete language with nine single-character commands (a b c d f 0 i j k), and use it to define 88 mathematical structures and a family tree of 65 theories that they model, with three aims: Pedagogy: It presents the mathematical structures in a unified way, with standardized presentation tableaus that define them and axiomatized theories that describe them. Connections: It highlights how they are related in the family tree via added symbols, axioms, etc. While the full tree is obviously infinite, its lower parts naturally separate into six main branches: the relational branch, the algebraic branch, the logic branch, the number branch, the set branch and the continuum branch. Foundations: The definitions, key theorems and models of each entry are verified in Lean. Mathematical structures are defined as equivalence classes of presentations, which in a constructivist spirit are defined in a simple, explicit and self-contained way in standardized presentation tableaus with minimal human baggage. For finite structures, the generating functions are defined by lookup tables. For countably infinite ones, they are instead defined computationally using MLISP, since more complex languages such as Lean are massive overkill for rigorously defining standard arithmetic operations (for example, the program "jibjbfid" defines subtraction). An interactive version is available at https://tegmark.org/mathtree. The Lean code is public, also verifies the correctness of MLISP and includes 43% of the theorems from Mathlib 2026-10-11. \end{abstract}

item.title: Verified Proof Refactoring with Codex and Qwen
item.dc:creator: Lazar Milikic, Gordan Đurić, Viktor Kunčak
item.description:
An LLM agent refactors existing Lean 4 proofs to shorten them and cut checking cost; every replacement is accepted only if Lean verifies it on all required versions.
We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the open-source Codex CLI to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements. The host keeps a replacement only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version. A deterministic CPU pass then refines the verified proofs. On the 60 problems in Lean Refactor Arena, model search achieves a local mean combined score of 82.07, and cleanup raises it to 82.18. The final proofs pass all 127 required proof–version checks. Our system placed first in the open-source LLM track of Lean Refactor Arena at VeriCodeGen.

item.title: The VC-Dimension of Visibility in Simple Polygons Is Six
item.dc:creator: Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled
item.description:
A Lean 4/Mathlib development verifies the VC-dimension upper bound against an axiomatic polygon interface, using geometric lemmas plus a RUP checker proved sound in Lean.
Six targets in a simple polygon can be placed so that, for every subset of the targets, some point in the polygon sees precisely that subset—that is, the polygon shatters the six targets. We prove that no simple polygon shatters seven targets. Together with Valtr's six-target construction, this determines the maximum visibility VC-dimension of a simple polygon to be six (even when the targets must lie in strictly convex position) and improves the previous upper bound of $14$ due to Gilbers and Klein. To rule out a shattered set of seven targets, we classify its convex-hull structure into $74$ cases. In each case, the absence of holes in the polygon forces visibility relations that we encode as Boolean constraints on links and triple orientations. Independently checkable SAT refutations exclude all $74$ cases. The upper-bound proof was derived using AI. A separate Lean 4 formalization independently verifies the upper bound against an axiomatic interface for simple polygons.

item.title: Density elimination for weakly commutative pseudo-uninorm logic:a correction and an explicit theory-level completeness proof
item.dc:creator: SanMin Wang
item.description:
The paper's main results on density elimination and standard completeness for pseudo-uninorm logic are formally verified in Lean 4, released as the GpsUL-1.0.0 artifact.
We correct the density-elimination argument for weakly commutative pseudo-uninorm logic in Wang, Symmetry 11 (2019), 368, retaining its basic ideas and overall strategy. The published definition of a labelled copy permits independent renamings of antecedent and succedent labels. Under the syntactic splicing interpretation used in that argument, a contraction-free derivable hypersequent and a four-element residuated chain refute the claimed compatibility of the resulting contraction with ordered density elimination. We require a single renaming on both sides of each closed block and prove that the linear rules and coherent closed-block contraction preserve provability of every member of the associated Cartesian families. An occurrence-based separation argument, together with normalization to cuts on the monoidal unit, establishes strong density elimination. We then derive standard completeness from density, retaining the original conclusion for formula theorems. For an explicit Hilbert presentation with independent conjugation parameters, we give a direct relative chain-countermodel proof for arbitrary theories in a countable language. Combined with the full bounded embedding of Wang (2026), this recovers the corresponding strong standard completeness result already stated there. The distinguished constant $f$, when present, is interpreted independently of the monoidal unit and the lattice bounds. The main results of this paper have been formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: An Order-Optimal Square-Root Bound for Online Maximin Share Allocation with Known Types
item.dc:creator: Zheyu Zhou
item.description:
The paper's numbered results, including the Θ(k^{-1/2}) guarantee and the antichain enumeration, are formalized in Lean 4.19 with Mathlib.
An allocator knows the indivisible goods, the number $n$ of agents, and the $k$ possible additive valuations. Each agent reveals their type on arrival and must immediately receive an irrevocable bundle. Kulkarni, Mehta, and Shahkar established a deterministic guarantee of $1/k$ of maximin share (MMS) and an upper bound of $2/(\sqrt{k}-2)$ for $k>4$. We determine the optimal order $Θ(k^{-1/2})$ by constructing a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, Single-or-Select. On every arrival sequence, it gives each agent a fraction $(1/\sqrt{2}-o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ of their truncated proportional share. This share dominates MMS and is the largest target $y$ for which the item values capped at $y$ sum to at least $ny$. By specializing the construction of Kulkarni et al. to two arrivals and counting its types exactly, we sharpen the upper bound to $(\sqrt{2}+o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ even for binary valuations. For two arrivals with binary valuations and every $k\ge2$, the optimal fraction is $1/p$, where $p$ is the largest integer with $1+\binom{2p}{2}\le k$. In particular, up to six binary types permit full maximin share. For two arbitrary additive types, a different polynomial-time algorithm guarantees $4/7$ of maximin share for any number of agents. This ratio is tight for the algorithm. With three arrivals and two types, the optimal deterministic fraction is exactly $9/10$. For randomized policies with $k$ known additive types, the optimal MMS fraction guaranteed to all agents with probability at least $1-δ$ on every fixed arrival sequence is $Θ(\max\{k^{-1/2},\sqrtδ\})$ for $0\leδ<1$.

item.title: Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs
item.dc:creator: Umut A. Acar, Eli Goldweber
item.description:
All theorems about entailment-graph search, frontiers, and ambiguity residue are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib over an arbitrary Boolean algebra.
Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.

item.title: A Hereditarily Atomic Domain without ACCP
item.dc:creator: Matthew Toeniskoetter
item.description:
The main theorems (a hereditarily atomic domain failing ACCP) and several variations are formalized in a companion Lean 4 library on GitHub.
An integral domain for which every subring is atomic is said to be hereditarily atomic. Every hereditarily atomic cancellative commutative monoid satisfies the ascending chain condition on principal ideals (ACCP), but it remained an open question whether every hereditarily atomic domain satisfies ACCP. We construct a hereditarily atomic domain which does not satisfy ACCP, answering this question in the negative. This domain is an overring of the ring of integer-valued polynomials $Int(\mathbb{Z})$, and its subrings that fail ACCP are precisely those of finite additive index.

item.title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
item.dc:creator: Luca Dall'Olio
item.description:
Cost certificates emitted by a Clang plugin are validated by a checker compiled from a Lean 4 definition proved sound, with mini-C semantics defined in Lean.
We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean 4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.

item.title: CrossCheck I: Cost Bounds of Imperative Programs as Constrained Optimization, with a Sound Cost Logic and a Verified Certificate Checker
item.dc:creator: Luca Dall'Olio
item.description:
Mechanizes the trace semantics, sound cost logic, and integer-arithmetic certificate checker in about 11,000 lines of Lean 4 over mathlib, with no sorry.
Static analysis of imperative programs often relies on iterative fixed-point approximations or concrete path exploration. We show that structured imperative control flow—while loops, linear recursion and branching recursion—can be mapped into constrained optimization problems over the free monoid of execution traces and the free algebra of computation trees. Ordering traces and trees by an intensional order-by-composition ($\sqsubseteq$), halting is characterized as finding the minimal trace or tree that satisfies the exit condition, and we prove that this characterization coincides with the standard big-step semantics. Exact state recurrences are undecidable in general, so we relax them into cost envelopes, using ranking potentials and the tropical $(\max,+)$ reading of the timing schema, and obtain sound upper bounds on execution cost. The bounds compose over whole programs in a cost logic for a small language with nondeterministic actions, procedures, recursion and assumed contracts, which we prove sound for terminating and non-terminating executions. A linear instance of the logic has certificates—programs annotated with invariants, potentials and Farkas multipliers—and a checker that validates them with integer arithmetic only; an accepted certificate bounds the cost of every execution. All results, the checker and the worked examples are machine-checked in Lean 4. A companion paper describes a Clang plugin that produces such certificates and its evaluation.

item.title: Quadratic periods after adjoining one move to a fixed subtraction game
item.dc:creator: Yuwen Pan
item.description:
Formalizes in Lean 4 the complete classification of periods and preperiods for subtraction game {3,6,17} plus one move, and Theorem 11.
Zhang conjectured that adjoining one move $c$ to a fixed subtraction set $S$ gives a Grundy sequence whose least preperiod and period are both $O_S(c)$. For every $q=20+9s$ with $s\ge0$, take $S=\{3,6,q-3\}$. Along $c=qk+1$ with $k\ge2$, the Grundy and win/loss sequences are periodic from heap zero with common least period $(k+2)(c+6)-11$, asymptotic to $c^2/q$. For $\{3,6,17\}$ we determine both least periods and preperiods for every positive $c$ and verify the complete table in Lean. Fixed bases with the same entire Grundy sequence realize infinitely many distinct positive quadratic coefficients for the augmented period. A second fixed triple gives a quadratic Grundy preperiod while the win/loss sequence repeats from heap zero. A third has a quadratic Grundy period but only a linear win/loss period. For an arbitrary fixed $S$, a linear bound on both Grundy invariants implies eventual affine formulas with integer coefficients on residue classes. The same finite-state method extends four numerical tables of Zhang. We also give the entire augmented sequence for $c>\max S$ when the losing heaps of $S$ are exactly the multiples of a fixed integer.

item.title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
item.dc:creator: Hao Xu, Kaiwen Yang, Jiacheng Qian, Yinuo Liu, Chih-Lin I
item.description:
Lean 4/Mathlib mechanization (49 modules, 19.7k lines) machine-checks 853 statements about HSFN addressing, routing, consensus, and reconfiguration results.
Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.

item.title: Towards a Formalised Framework for Analog Electronics and Circuit Theory
item.dc:creator: Yaohua Zhang, Zhi Kai Pong
item.description:
Formalises an ideal RC low-pass filter in Lean 4 with Mathlib, defining impedance and component models and proving voltage division and transfer-function theorems.
Circuit theory provides the mathematical foundation for the analysis and design of electronic circuits. However, conventional circuit derivations often rely on assumptions and mathematical relationships that are not explicitly recorded, making their verification and reuse challenging. In this paper, we present the first step towards a formalised framework for circuit theory and analog electronics using the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover. As a proof of concept, we formalise an ideal RC low-pass filter, establishing reusable definitions for component impedance and circuit connections, and machine-checked theorems for voltage division, the transfer function, and low-pass behaviour. Building upon this demonstration, we outline a broader vision for an extensible library of circuit models, definitions, and verified results. Our long-term aim is to digitise, standardise, and verify circuit theory, enabling established knowledge to be systematically checked, shared, and reused across different circuit analyses.

item.title: Linear entanglement suffices for $f$-routing
item.dc:creator: Kevin Bogner
item.description:
Main theorem (2n+2 EPR pairs suffice for f-routing) is formalized in Lean using only standard axioms; code on GitHub, written by an AI model.
In $f$-routing, Alice receives an $n$-bit string $x$ and an unknown qubit, and Bob receives an $n$-bit string $y$. They share a state prepared in advance and exchange one simultaneous message each.
