The party selected by the Boolean function $f(x,y)$ must then recover the unknown qubit without further communication. To perform $f$-routing successfully, Alice and Bob need to share entanglement that scales with $n$ for some functions $f$, but the lower and upper bounds for the entanglement are not tight. This paper shows that $2n+2$ shared EPR pairs suffice for every function $f$. The best previous bound that holds for all functions is a shared state of $2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$ qubits. The new strategy moves the cost from the shared state to the messages: Alice sends an exponentially long message of $2^{n+1}+1$ qubits, while Bob sends only classical bits. When the messages are counted towards the resources as well, the previous strategy remains the cheapest known. The result also limits lower bounds that count only the shared state: they cannot exceed a linear number of EPR pairs. The result is formalized in Lean.

item.title: Depth Hierarchies for Symmetric Algebraic Circuits
item.dc:creator: Anuj Dawar, Prateek Dwivedi, Benedikt Pago, Tim Seppelt
item.description:
Main results, including the depth hierarchy theorems, definitions of symmetric circuits/ABPs and symVNP, are formalised in Lean with an archived artifact.
Algebraic complexity studies the cost of computing families of polynomials by algebraic circuits, with the central goal of proving super-polynomial circuit lower bounds and separations between different models of algebraic computation. Since such lower bounds remain elusive for general circuits, a common strategy is to focus on restricted models. A recent line of work (ICALP 2020, ITCS & STOC 2026) introduces and studies symmetry as a syntactic circuit restriction, showing exponential symmetric lower bounds for the permanent, as well as separations between symmetric analogues of algebraic formulas ($\mathsf{VF}$), skew circuits ($\mathsf{VS}$), and circuits ($\mathsf{VP}$). We investigate the role of depth as a complexity parameter in symmetric circuits. For every fixed $Δ\geq 1$, we exhibit a family of polynomials computable by symmetric circuits of polynomial size and depth $2Δ+3$, but requiring size $n^{Ω(\log n)}$ at depth $Δ$. We also define symmetric versions of the bounded-depth algebraic complexity classes $\mathsf{VAC}^k$, for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, that we call $\mathsf{symVAC}^k$, and establish two strict hierarchies: Firstly, a hierarchy within $\mathsf{symVAC}^0$, and secondly, a hierarchy of the form $\mathsf{symVAC}^k \subsetneq \mathsf{symVAC}^{k+1}$ for all $k$. The latter shows that symmetric circuits of depth $(\log n)^{k+1}$ are strictly more powerful than depth-$(\log n)^k$ circuits. Moreover, we place the bounded-depth classes within the landscape of symmetric algebraic complexity developed by Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt (STOC 2026). We complement this picture by introducing $\mathsf{symVNP}$, a symmetric analogue of $\mathsf{VNP}$, and establishing $\mathsf{symVNP}$-completeness of the permanent under symmetric projections.

item.title: Sharpness of the Martin-O'Bryant autoconvolution inequality
item.dc:creator: Tonći Crmarić, Vjekoslav Kovač, Jelena Rupčić
item.description:
Theorem 1, that the autoconvolution ratio supremum equals 1, was formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the formal proof was produced with ChatGPT.
We show that there does not exist a constant $c<1$ such that ${\lVert f\ast f\rVert}_{L^{2}}^2\le c\,{\lVert f\ast f\rVert}_{L^{1}}{\lVert f\ast f\rVert}_{L^{\infty}}$ holds for every nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\cap L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

item.title: Quantitative homogenization for the critical long-range random conductance model
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Bou-Rabee, Paul Dario
item.description:
Every labeled theorem, lemma and proposition is formalized in Lean 4 from Mathlib and the Lattice-Probability library, with the formalization written by Claude.
We consider the long-range random conductance model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ at the critical exponent: the jump rate between sites $x$ and $y$ is $\mathbf{a}(\{x,y\}) |x-y|^{-(d+2)}$, where the conductances $\mathbf{a}(\{x,y\})$ are independent, uniformly elliptic and have a common mean. Below the critical exponent $(d+2)$ the walk converges to a stable process; above it, to Brownian motion with diffusive $\sqrt{t}$ scaling. At criticality the second moment of the jump kernel diverges logarithmically. We establish quantitative homogenization of the associated heat equation at the rate $1/\sqrt{|\ln \varepsilon|}$. As a consequence, we deduce annealed convergence of the random walk to Brownian motion under the anomalous $\sqrt{t \log t}$ scaling. Unlike in standard homogenization, the effective diffusivity is determined by the mean conductance alone, with no corrector contribution at leading order.

item.title: The Algebraic Landscape of Kochen-Specker Sets in Dimension Three
item.dc:creator: Michael Kernaghan
item.description:
Lean 4 with Mathlib kernel-checks the roots-of-unity uncolorability theorem, the 45-word circle uncolorability, and minimum KS subset sizes for six pools.
The classic three-dimensional Kochen-Specker (KS) proofs take their ray coordinates from a small set of numbers: {0, +-1, +-sqrt(2)} for the 33 rays of Peres and {0, +-1, +-2} for the 31 rays of Conway and Kochen. We treat that set, the coordinate alphabet, as a parameter. An alphabet generates a finite pool of rays, and the pool is or is not KS-uncolorable. We determine the uncolorable alphabets in four families. (A) Two-symbol alphabets {0, +-1, +-x}, x complex: uncolorable only when x or 1/x is +-2, +-sqrt(2), +-sqrt(-2), or x is a primitive third or sixth root of unity; no KS set with such coordinates has fewer than 31 rays. (B) Real three-symbol alphabets {0, +-1, +-x, +-y} with 1 < x < y: uncolorable exactly when two letters have ratio 2 or sqrt(2), or at eight further points; again no KS set has fewer than 31 rays. (C) Conjugate-closed alphabets {0, +-1, +-x, +-x*}: uncolorable exactly when |x|^2 = 2, or |x|^2 = 1/2, or x*/x is a primitive third or sixth root of unity, or x is +-2 or +-1/2. The uncolorable alphabets are therefore not isolated. On the circle |x|^2 = 2 a fixed list of 45 words is uncolorable at every point, and no shorter fixed list is; the circle |x|^2 = 1/2 carries the 33-ray family of Gould and Aravind. (D) The pool of 0 and the n-th roots of unity is uncolorable if and only if 6 divides n. Minimum KS subsets are certified by exact computation for eleven named pools. The Lean proof assistant checks (D) for n >= 3, the uncolorability of the 45 words at every point of the circle, and the minima 31, 33, 33, 33, 43 and 47 of six pools. This version replaces the classification by "cancellation mechanisms" and "islands" proposed in versions 1-9, which did not survive checking; an appendix lists the withdrawn claims, among them a golden-ratio minimum of 52 (a 51-ray set exists).

item.title: A $(17/7-o(1))n$ Circuit Lower Bound for Binary-Encoded 3-SAT
item.dc:creator: Theodoros Yianni, Sahibzada Allahyar
item.description:
Lean 4 with Mathlib formalizes the finite inequality and asymptotic 17/7 circuit lower bound for arbitrary acyclic binary circuits, archived on Zenodo.
We strengthen the elementary $n-1$ circuit lower bound for a specified binary encoding of 3-SAT to $(17/7)n-O(n\log\log n/\log n)$ gates over the full two-input Boolean basis, with unrestricted depth and sharing. For each integer $w\ge5$, we encode 3-CNF formulas with exactly $m=2^w-1$ clauses over $m$ available variables using $n=3m(w+1)$ bits. The proof embeds Boolean tests in variable identifiers while retaining $n-o(n)$ free bits, and combines weighted gate elimination with a nonlinear-gate lower bound from the tests' full algebraic degree over $\mathbb F_2$. We provide Lean proofs of the finite inequality and the asymptotic bound for arbitrary acyclic binary circuits.

item.title: Linear forms in logarithms of rational numbers: an ineffective measure with the best possible exponent
item.dc:creator: Gregory V. Chudnovsky
item.description:
The main theorem and corollary on linear forms in logarithms are fully verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with sources in ancillary files and declaration names cited throughout.
Let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be positive rational numbers without a nontrivial multiplicative relation. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a constant $C>0$, not effective, such that $|h_0+h_1\log a_1+\dots+h_n\log a_n| \ge C\max(1,|h_0|,\dots,|h_n|)^{-n-\varepsilon}$ for all integers $h_0,\dots,h_n$, not all zero. The exponent $n$ is best possible. For $n=1$ this is the known fact that the irrationality exponent of $\log a$ is $2$; for $h_0=0$ it gives the exponent $n$ for the linear forms $h_1\log a_1+\dots+h_n\log a_n$. The proof is an induction on $n$, starting from $n=1$. The step from $n-1$ to $n$ logarithms uses an interpolation determinant on $\mathbb{G}_m^n\times\mathbb{G}_a$ at the multiples of a rational point, in the manner of arXiv:2610.28079; its geometric part, a curve inequality, is proved by a second induction, on the number of torus coordinates, with the two-torus inequality of arXiv:2610.28079 as the base. The method is the interpolation and determinant method of OpenAI's preprint on the irrationality exponent of $π$; the case $n=1$ was obtained earlier by Liu, Jiang and Zhang (arXiv:2610.10192). The theorem and its corollary are verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the sources are in the ancillary files, on top of the Lean supplement of arXiv:2610.28079. This paper follows the formal proof: every definition, constant and intermediate statement is given in the form in which it is formalized, with the name of the Lean declaration.

item.title: The limit shape of uniform random antichains in $[0,1]^d$
item.dc:creator: Andrew Elvey Price, Minjae Park
item.description:
An AI-generated Lean formalization of the main results is provided in an accompanying repository; the authors reviewed the formal statements of the main theorems.
For each $d\ge2$, we study $n$ independent uniform points in $[0,1]^d$, conditioned to form an antichain: no point is strictly smaller than another in every coordinate. We prove that the point cloud converges in Hausdorff distance to the closure of the hypersurface \[\mathcal S_d=\left\{\mathbf x\in(0,1)^d: \sum_{i=1}^dΦ^{-1}(\mathbf x_i)=0\right\}\] in probability as $n\to\infty$, where $Φ$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The proof also shows that the antichain probability $a_n$ satisfies $\log a_n=-\frac{n}{d-1}\log n+β_d n+o(n)$ for a finite constant $β_d$. We identify the limiting empirical distribution and hence the limiting permuton of uniform random $d$-dimensional permutations avoiding a single pattern of size $2$.

item.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
item.dc:creator: Ruichen Qiu, Hao Shen, Lihong Zhi, Xiao-Shan Gao
item.description:
Builds a benchmark of 197 Lean declaration sets from 18 real Lean projects, reconstructed under Lean 4.34.1, for reviewing informal-formal semantic alignment.
Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. LeanReviewBench provides a testbed for reviewing semantic correspondence in existing mathematical formalization projects. LeanReviewBench is available at https://github.com/MechMath/LeanReviewBench.

item.title: The Hlawka-Schatten inequality: an exposition of recent progress
item.dc:creator: Seokbin Lee
item.description:
Exposits AI-produced Lean 4 formalizations of Hlawka-Schatten results, deriving its proof presentation from the Lean code and Prove2Me missions.
We give an expository account of recent progress on a question of Audenaert and Kittaneh concerning a Hlawka-type inequality for Schatten norms of matrices. We review the classical Hornich-Hlawka inequality and explain the motivation behind understanding the so-called Hlawka-Schatten inequality. We present an elementary $2 \times 2$ construction showing that no finite constant satisfies the Hlawka-Schatten inequality for the trace norm, and explain Esa's proof that a dimension-independent constant exists for every $1 < p < \infty$. We also discuss the Hlawka-Schatten inequality for diagonal matrices and subsequent developments thereof on Prove2Me. Our aim is to make the mathematical ideas behind these AI-assisted results accessible, and to clarify their relationship with the available Lean formalizations.

item.title: Quantum Subentropy: Subadditivity and Sharp Bounds on Discrimination Error
item.dc:creator: Pratik Patil
item.description:
All theoretical results on quantum subentropy are formalized in Lean 4, partly adapting code from the Omega Institute's Lean development.
Subentropy gives a tight spectral lower bound on the accessible information of ensembles of pure states. We prove its subadditivity for arbitrary bipartite states in finite dimensions and derive a sharp relation between conditional subentropy and the minimum discrimination error. This relation strengthens a conjectured comparison with conditional min-entropy. Its inverse gives the strongest universal lower bound on the error determined only by conditional subentropy and the number of labels. Both main results follow from a comparison of conditional subentropy with the average subentropy of measurement posteriors, valid for mixed signal states and every finite measurement. We characterize all equality cases in these two results and bound posterior deviations near equality. We also determine the optimal Lipschitz constant in trace distance for conditional subentropy on classical-quantum states, including the exact constant when the quantum marginal is fixed. A determinant inequality strengthens subadditivity and proves strong subadditivity for classical distributions, while an exact counterexample shows that strong subadditivity fails for quantum states. Lean 4 proofs of all theoretical results are available at https://pratikpatil.io/lean/subentropy/

item.title: StatClaim: Study Designs as Types, Protocols as Programs and Statistical Claims as Proof Obligations
item.dc:creator: Supun Manathunga
item.description:
Lean is the verification backend: generated proof obligations for Type I error, familywise error, power and coverage claims are proved and checked in Lean.
Statistical guarantees depend on the compatibility of a study's model, hypotheses, sampling plan and analysis. StatClaim is a declarative domain-specific language for encoding research protocols and statistical analysis plans as programs built from objects whose types encode their statistical roles within the study design. The compiler checks type compatibility and applies contracts to check additional requirements on the values and relationships of these objects. When verification is requested, StatClaim's backend constructs and checks proofs of supported statistical claims using Lean under stated assumptions. These claims concern Type I error, familywise error, power and interval coverage, including supported combinations of analyses and procedures with planned stopping rules. Reports distinguish formally proved, conditional, cited and author-declared guarantees and provide replayable certificates for verified claims. The same specification supports sample-size searches, power calculations and interval-precision assessment using exact calculations, analytical approximations or reproducible simulation. A command-line interface, editor integration and graphical block editor use a shared compiler and execution layer. Validation reproduces 102 optimal and minimax two-stage designs from Simon's published tables and verifies their error and power bounds in Lean. A clinical trial case study illustrates partial encoding of a published analysis plan using cited methods and conditional proofs. The open-source implementation includes runnable tutorials and examples for specifying and checking study designs before outcomes are collected.
